Chapter 2. Understanding the Mind and Ego—Breaking Free from Old Patterns.
Once you start practicing presence, something interesting happens. You quickly notice that your mind isn’t just a problem-solving machine. It’s also the source of all those old habits and routines that shape how you see yourself and the world around you.
The mind loves to build a sense of identity out of your thoughts, memories, and the roles you play. That’s what we often call the ego. But here’s the thing—ego isn’t some solid, unchanging thing. It’s more like a bundle of mental habits that make you feel separate or not quite enough.
The ego feeds on comparison, on judging yourself and others, and on always needing to be right. It digs through your past to construct a story about who you are and what you deserve. And most of the time, that story is colored by a sense of “not quite there yet.” The ego doesn’t like to settle into the present moment. It’s always chasing future achievements, or holding onto old grudges. And that’s what creates that low-level anxiety and restlessness we all know too well.
Think about someone waiting for a promotion at work. The mind starts replaying old disappointments or daydreaming about being recognized down the line, but it almost never lands on simply being present with the task at hand. The ego whispers, “You’re not valued unless you get this.” And suddenly, just doing your job feels tense and unsatisfying.
So, how do you break free from these old patterns? It all starts with awareness. When you notice your thoughts and emotions—without instantly reacting or identifying with them—you create a little space. And in that space, you realize: thoughts aren’t facts. The story your mind tells isn’t the whole truth about who you are.
There are a few practical ways to open up that space:
First, try witnessing your thoughts. Pay attention to those recurring patterns, especially the ones that fire up strong emotions. Imagine you’re watching a play, just observing the drama instead of getting pulled into it.
Next, start naming the ego. When you catch yourself defending, comparing, or judging, silently note, “Ah, that’s just my ego at work.” This simple act of recognition actually softens its grip.
And whenever your mind drags you back into old stories, gently come back to the present. Tune in to your senses. Notice what’s right in front of you, right now.
Over time, you’ll see that the mind and ego aren’t enemies you need to fight. They’re just natural parts of being human—things you can understand and even move beyond. The goal isn’t to stop thinking altogether, but to change your relationship with your thoughts. You want to use your mind as a tool, instead of letting it run the show.
As this new relationship with your mind takes shape, you’ll start to notice more peace, more freedom. The urge to prove yourself or compare to others just fades away. In its place, there’s a quiet confidence that comes from being truly present. And that presence isn’t passive—it’s an alert, open awareness that lets you experience life in all its richness, right as it unfolds.
